transcript.content: Hello. I am Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Well, I suppose... gosh, where do I even start? I mean, I've been struggling a bit in general, just feeling rather low, but I came in today because... well, even on my better days, the days where I can actually get up and get myself put together and out of the house, I just can't shake this awful feeling. 

It's about the people at my church—I've been going to the same congregation for over thirty years, mind you, ever since my husband and I bought our house—and also the ladies in my Tuesday morning walking club. We usually walk around the indoor mall before the shops open, just to keep our joints moving. But lately, I can just tell they are watching me. And it's not just the staring, it's... well, they put these little messages about me in things. 

Like at church, in the Sunday bulletin, I'll be sitting in the pew reading the weekly announcements or the prayer list, and I can see these hidden remarks that are clearly, specifically directed at me. And then at the walking club, it's the exact same thing. They'll be talking, just chatting about the weather or their gardens, but I can hear it in what they say. They slip these little messages about me right into their sentences, disguised as normal conversation. Even when my mood is a little lighter and I'm trying to just enjoy the walk or the church service, I just can't ignore it. It makes me so uncomfortable, always having to read between the lines, and I don't understand why they've all decided to do this to me. So... I guess that's why I'm here. It's just exhausting.
Aside from the hidden meanings you perceive in their words, do you ever hear voices when no one else is around?

Well, yes... yes, I suppose I do. It’s the strangest thing, Dr. Smith. You see, when the house gets completely quiet—you know, no television on, no radio playing, just that heavy sort of silence you get in the mid-afternoon? I'll just be sitting in my armchair in the living room, maybe doing a bit of cross-stitch or just resting my eyes because my energy has been so terribly low lately, and... well, I will hear my name. 

Just out of the blue. Or sometimes it's a few words, like a partial sentence. And the thing that really gets me is that it's not just some random sound, it's actually in my friend's voice. Usually one of the ladies from the walking club. I'll hear it coming right from the kitchen, or sometimes out on the back porch. 

And it is so clear, so perfectly normal and clear, that I don't even think twice about it. I actually answer back! I'll call out, "I'm in the living room!" or "Did you need something?" and I'll put my sewing down and get all the way up to go look. And it's only when I get to the kitchen doorway that I stop and remember... well, nobody is there. The doors are locked. But I swear to you, in that moment, it sounds exactly like they are standing right there by my refrigerator talking to me. It gives me such a start, my heart just pounds, because I really thought they had come over, and then I'm just standing there alone in the quiet again.

When you look back over the last few months, have these feelings of low energy and sadness been present every single day, even on the days when you aren't feeling particularly worried about the messages from your friends?

Well, yes, Doctor... yes, I suppose they have. It’s hard to untangle it all sometimes, you know? But when I really sit down and think about it, look back over the last... oh, gosh, it must be months now. Since before Thanksgiving, certainly. My sister called around then, and I just couldn't even bring myself to chat about the turkey or the stuffing, which is so unlike me because I usually host, you see. 

But yes, to answer your question, even on the days when the ladies at the walking club aren't putting those awful hidden meanings into their sentences about their hydrangeas, or when I don't hear my name being called from the empty kitchen... even then, this heavy, awful feeling is just sitting right there on my chest. It's like a damp blanket that I just can't throw off. The sadness is always there, just humming away in the background. And the guilt! Oh, the guilt is terrible. I'll sit in my chair and just feel so terribly guilty about not keeping the house up the way my late husband liked it, or not calling my sister back. 

And I just don't care about the things I used to. The cross-stitch I mentioned? I used to make the most beautiful ornaments for the church bazaar. Every year, people would ask for them. But now, my basket just sits there. I look at the thread and I just... I don't care. Even when my mind isn't racing with what the Sunday bulletin really meant, or who might be standing on the back porch, I still just can't find the joy in the thread. So, yes, for most of this whole long stretch, that terrible sadness and the guilt and just not caring about my little hobbies... it's all been right there in the background, plain as day, even when the other things are quiet. It's just so draining, Dr. Smith. I used to have so much energy, you know. I'd be up at dawn, baking...
Have there been any periods of at least two weeks where you felt your mood was relatively normal, but you were still experiencing these thoughts about the bulletin or hearing those voices?

Well, yes, actually... now that you mention it, there was a time. It was, oh, maybe right around the beginning of February? The weather was just starting to turn a little less bitter, and I remember thinking that maybe, just maybe, the worst of the winter slump was behind me. For a few weeks there—maybe three or four weeks, if I'm remembering right—the heaviness actually lifted a bit. I wasn't feeling quite so weighed down by that terrible sadness, and the guilt wasn't pressing on me quite so hard. 

I was actually getting up and getting dressed properly, putting on a nice blouse instead of just my housecoat, and I was even eating a bit better. I made a proper pot roast one Sunday, with the carrots and the potatoes just the way I like them, which I hadn't done in months. I thought, "Oh, finally, I'm getting back to my old self." 

But the strange thing, Dr. Smith, the really confusing part of it all, is that even during those few weeks when my mood was so much better and I had a bit more spring in my step... the other things didn't go away at all. I was still sitting in my armchair in the afternoon, feeling perfectly content, and I would still hear my friend's voice calling my name from the kitchen. Clear as a bell. And I'd still get up and look, and no one would be there. 

And I still went to church those weeks, feeling quite proud of myself for getting there early, but the moment I opened the Sunday bulletin, there they were—those same little hidden remarks, those hints about me tucked right into the announcements about the choir practice and the bake sale. It was so frustrating! Because I felt so much better in myself, you know, my spirit felt lighter, but I still had to deal with the ladies at the walking club slipping those messages into their chatter about their grandchildren. So yes, there was definitely a spell of several weeks where the sadness took a back seat, but the voices and the hints... they stayed right there with me the whole time.
